title: field-ask-validator-script-for-sla-commitments
content:
Purpose and scope
This is a sales/field-facing working script and procurement checklist to validate buyer asks for Dedicated GPU capacity. It’s intentionally pragmatic — short decision trees, sample contract language, and pushback scripts for common procurement tradeoffs (isolation vs. cost, latency SLOs vs. throughput guarantees). Use this when a customer brings a draft RFP / SOW asking for guaranteed throughput and isolation.

TL;DR (what to get to fast)
- Confirm the buyer’s critical metric: p95 latency OR sustained throughput (reqs in RPS / tokens/sec).
- Validate whether they need hard isolation (no multi-tenant GPUs) or logical isolation with guaranteed capacity slices.
- Offer the three-tier fallback: Dedicated reserved pool -> Reserved + burst -> Cross-region fallback with warm standby.
- Give procurement a concise contract snippet they can drop into their SOW to get a commercial yes.

Buyer profile quick-mapping
- Platform Architects (throughput first): care about deterministic concurrency, queueing behavior, and autoscale windows.
- Security/Infosec (isolation first): care about tenancy, KMS/HSM, audit logs, and breach blast radius.
- Finance (cost predictability): wants committed spend, unit economics, and credits for underutilization.
- Product/ML infra (latency/SLA): cares about p95/p99 latency, cold-start behavior, cache priming.

Key positioning pillars (plain language)
1) Predictable throughput: We back committed capacity with a throughput SLO. Not a vague promise — we quantify it as sustained tokens/sec per minute over a rolling window and provide reconciliation reports monthly.
2) Tenant isolation: We offer single-tenant GPU pools plus network-level VPC isolation and optional on-prem installers for air-gapped needs.
3) Measured latency SLOs: For interactive workloads we publish p95 latency targets at specific sequence lengths; for batch workloads we guarantee sustained throughput.
4) Procurement-ready guardrails: We provide boilerplate SOW clauses, defined escalation SLAs, and credit formulas for any SLO breaches.

Competitive differentiation notes (how to win objections)
- Against public cloud endpoints: They’ll point to raw GPU access and price flexibility. Counter: public cloud lacks the pre-optimized serving runtime, automatic KV/prefix caching and inference-specific batching optimizations that reduce per-token cost for real traffic shapes. We show customer-case delta numbers (usually 20–40% unit cost improvement on similar models).
- Against self-hosted inference stacks: They’ll point to control and lower op-ex costs at scale. Counter: the operational burden and unpredictability of tail latency during traffic spikes is real; we offer SLA-backed behavior plus dedicated SRE support and automated rollbacks.
- Against other inference vendors: They may offer similar SLA language. Counter: our observable proofs — token-level billing, per-route tail-latency traces, and rollback/time-based canary—are the differentiators in procurement conversations.

Field script: qualifying questions (fast)
1) What is your expected 95th percentile latency requirement for interactive calls (ms) and for what sequence length?
2) What steady-state throughput (tokens/sec or requests/sec) do you expect during peak business hours?
3) Do you require physical GPU tenancy or is network/VPC isolation sufficient?
4) What are the hard stop dates for procurement/contract execution? (SLOs often lose to legal timelines)
5) What failure modes worry you most? noisy neighbors, credential exfil, cold starts?

Objection handling snippets
- "We need single-tenant hardware for compliance": Great — we can provide single-tenant GPU pools with dedicated provisioning lead times. Ask: is certification or attestation required (e.g., SOC2/AICPA, FedRAMP)? If yes, route to enterprise team and provide timeline.
- "We can self-host cheaper": Ask for their end-to-end TCO assumptions. Offer a joint TCO review comparing ops headcount, incident MTTR, and model refresh costs. Share a conservative Redwood-run example showing ops delta over 12 months.
- "We need hard latency SLOs for public traffic": We’ll map their traffic profile and propose a mix of pinned capacity for interactive paths + lower-cost scalable pools for non-critical batched calls.

Procurement checklist (what to attach to SOW quickly)
- Define capacity: GPUs (type), reserved slots, and guaranteed sustained tokens/sec.
- SLA metrics: p95/p99 latency for defined sequence lengths, and throughput SLO across a rolling 1-hour window.
- Credits: linear credit schedule tied to % breach and duration (example language below).
- Isolation & security: tenancy model, VPC peering, KMS/HSM integration, audit log retention period.
- Support & escalation: Tier, response times, named CSM/SE contact, security escalation path.
- Term & payment: commitment term (12/24/36 months), termination windows, and underutilization credits.

Sample contract language (drop-in)
- "Committed Throughput": Provider commits to a sustained throughput of X tokens/sec on average over any continuous 60-minute window. If measured throughput falls below 90% of the committed level for more than 15 minutes, Customer shall be eligible for service credits calculated as Y% of the monthly fee for each hour of breach, capped at Z%.
- "Isolation": Provider will provision dedicated GPU capacity for the Customer with no co-tenanted inference jobs on the same hardware. Network isolation will be enforced via VPC peering and customer-managed firewall rules.

Operational redlines & lead times
- Lead time for single-tenant GPU provisioning: 6–8 weeks for standard configs, longer for specialized hardware.
- Autoscale window tuning: changes to burst capacity or quota take up to 72 hours to validate in production.
- Model onboarding SLA: initial model validation and baseline perf benchmarks within 5 business days of receiving model artifact.

Evidence pack (what to show procurement)
- Monthly reconciliation report: per-route throughput, p95/p99 latencies, token consumption.
- Benchmarks: synthetic and customer-like traces showing per-token cost delta vs cloud-hosted endpoints.
- Post-incident reports: anonymized examples of incident mitigation, rollback timelines, and MTTR.

Negotiation playbook (concessions and counters)
- Concession: reduce base price for first 3 months in exchange for a 12-month commitment and a ≥75% utilization target.
- Counter: if customer wants physical tenancy at lower price, require a 24-month commit and accelerate provisioning with a one-time setup fee.
- Risk transfer: optional SLA tiers — bronze (best-effort), silver (throughput-backed), gold (throughput + latency backed with higher credits). Use gold only for enterprise deals with exec signoff.

Open questions / things to validate with Product & Legal
- Exact credit formulas for mixed breaches (throughput + latency simultaneous).
- Audit artifact retention needs beyond standard retention periods for regulated customers.
- Specific GPU SKUs and BOM for single-tenant offerings (we need procurement to lock lead times).

Next steps for field reps
- Run the Qualifying Questions during discovery call and fill the one-pager that attaches to the RFP.
- If single-tenant is requested, open an intake ticket with Release Eng + Infra for capacity planning.
- Share the sample contract snippet with procurement and ask for redlines; feed redlines back to Legal as a single consolidated doc.

Notes to self / messy bits (working doc style)
- Need one-pager TCO calculator (input: cluster hours, ops FTEs, incident rate). TODO: Marcus to draft.
- Bench numbers: pull last three customer post-mortems with throughput numbers anonymized.
- Add a short appendix with example telemetry screenshots (Console -> per-route latency) for next revision.

Appendix: short firing examples to include in demos
- Demo 1: Show warm vs cold KV cache impact on p95 by hitting a route with a warm prefix cache.
- Demo 2: Show how cross-region fallback flips within 120s when capacity alarm fires (explain warm standby concept).

End.
